newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FCC says adopted digital television standard.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FCC says adopted digital television standard.

text.p: U.S. Federal Communications Commission said on Thursday it voted Dec. 24 to approve a technology standard for a new generation of high-definition digital television.
The standard is based on a compromise agreed upon last month by the broadcast, consumer electronics and computer industries, FCC said.

Digital TV offers crystal-clear pictures and CD-quality sound. It is expected to promote a "computer friendly" TV system that allows viewers to watch programs while surfing the Internet over the same "smart box."
The FCC said the standard it adopted would allow for transmission of one or two high-resolution programs or up to five standard shows on a single existing channel.
But the FCC said it would decide later on a possible re-allocation of channels.

Broadcasters holding licenses to existing channels argued that they should be allowed to keep their rights and gain control over the new channel subdivisions. Some legislators and companies seeking licenses favord starting from scratch and auctioning off the new channels.
The new standard does not take a position on picture size and quality, one of the most contentious issues involved.
Television manufacturers wanted a standard imposing a broadcast technique known as "interlacing", used in existing TV sets, that updates every other line of a picture on each pass.
The computer industry argued that this format would stifle the converegence of TV and computer technologies.
They sought a standard imposing "progressive scanning", used in computer monitors today, which updates every line of the picture on each pass.
The new standard "provides a springboard for global leadership in high definition digital equipment and programming," commissioner Susan Ness said in a statement.
Ness added that the new standard, by improving the quality of broadcast images, would bolster broadcasters in their competition with cable and satellite services that already offer digital pictures.
"Consumers should not have to settle for a second-rate free broadcast service," she said.
